01 / E‑INVEST · TRADING PLATFORM

Trust had to be
rebuilt before trading.

The redesign started with a legacy app, real customer feedback and the decision to turn repeated friction into a clearer investment experience.

Role
UX research, product design, UI
Platforms
Mobile & web
Scope
Trading, portfolio & order flows
Original redesigned mobile UI

/ 01

THE BRIEF

Not a new coat of paint.
A new point of view.

The existing product supported the mechanics of trading, but customers struggled with the experience around it: portfolio visibility, chart precision, order management and a reliable path through high-stakes actions.

ContextLegacy trading app already delivered to a bank
ChallengeRestore clarity without reducing market depth
OutcomeA unified direction for mobile and web

/ 02

THE STARTING POINT

The legacy app was already telling us what had to change.

The redesign did not begin with a visual direction. It began with the live product and the feedback customers left when access, portfolio visibility, precision and trade control were not working for them.

01

Access could fail before a customer even entered.

Password and login issues became a direct break in trust.

02

Precision was not optional.

Customers called out rounded chart values when exact share prices mattered.

03

Portfolio visibility was incomplete.

People could not always see holdings, history, dividends or dependable P&L context.

04

Orders needed clearer control.

Filtering, sorting, status and the journey after selling required more guidance.

Original customer feedback from the legacy application · the evidence that initiated the redesign

/ 03

FROM CUSTOMER SIGNAL TO DESIGN PRIORITY

The reviews showed recurring friction. The redesign grouped it into three product priorities.

Account confidence

Make account access, holdings and portfolio status easier to find and understand.

Decision precision

Show share prices and market context with the detail customers expect.

Trade control

Make order states easier to find, review and follow through the trade journey.

/ 04

DESIGN STRATEGY

Not a feature checklist.
A framework for better decisions.

01

Visibility before action

Put portfolio state, market movement and order status where customers can evaluate them before trading.

02

Precision by default

Respect financial data: exact prices, contextual charts and readable performance signals.

03

One coherent journey

Connect discovery, analysis, execution and confirmation rather than scattering decision-making across the product.

Customer signalDesign response
Portfolio and account information lacked a clear hierarchyDesigned a scannable home state with balance, market pulse and useful shortcuts.
Market details were hard to interpret quicklyFocused the stock view around price, change, chart range and actionable data.
High-stakes trade states needed reassuranceMade review and confirmation explicit, with relevant order information in context.

/ 05

MOBILE EXPERIENCE

From onboarding
to focused decisions.

The new mobile direction makes the full investment journey legible: set up access, understand the account, scan the market, analyze a symbol and review the action before confirming.

/ 06

THE WEB DIRECTION

Detail when it matters.
Hierarchy everywhere.

The same decision framework extends to the desktop product: a high-density trading environment where navigation, order detail, charts and market context remain readable.

WEB PRODUCT FOCUS
  • Markets & price context
  • Portfolio visibility
  • Order status & control
  • Trading detail
DESIGN PRINCIPLE

Density without noise.

Information is deliberately grouped into stable areas of focus: navigation, market context, active position and decision controls.

/ 07

REFLECTION

More than a visual refresh.

Customer feedback grounded

The work begins with real customer pain points and turns those signals into an experience strategy.

System-wide

Mobile and web follow one shared logic rather than becoming separate product stories.

Decision-led

Every screen is accountable to a moment where clarity, trust or control matters.

02 / 7SALTY · FINTECH

Micro-savings,
made accessible.

A micro-savings product shaped around the needs, trust barriers and everyday financial habits of its audience.

← Back to portfolio

PROJECT OVERVIEW

A micro-savings product designed for financial inclusion.

7salty is a micro-saving application created to help a wider population save money and participate in the financial system—particularly low-income people and youth.

50,000 LE

Maximum account balance

0 LE

Minimum balance required

Free

No charges to use the service

THE PROBLEM

Saving solutions often exclude the people who need them most.

01

Minimum balance

Low-income individuals cannot maintain the required minimum balances.

02

High fees

Maintenance and transaction fees erode small savings.

03

Low interest

Minimal returns on small balances offer little incentive to save.

04

Operational capacity

Banks struggle to manage a high volume of small transactions.

UX RESEARCH

Learn the saving behaviors before designing the solution.

The goal was to understand the needs, frustrations and opportunities around a fintech micro-saving solution.

06

User interviews

Four low-income users and two service providers.

57

Survey responses

To understand target-audience behavior and thinking.

18–30

Core study range

Participants included employees, housewives, students and workers.

RESEARCH OBJECTIVES

Start by understanding the saving context—not by assuming a feature list.

  1. 01

    Explore how low-income people experience saving and the barriers they meet in existing financial services.

  2. 02

    Identify user needs, frustrations and opportunities that could shape a new fintech micro-saving solution.

SURVEY EVIDENCE

The research made the opportunity measurable.

Three signals clarified where trust, saving motivation and financial habits needed more attention.

44%

25 participants did not trust online payment.

57%

33 participants saved money through other means.

43%

24 participants saved money in a bank account.

The evidence supported a product direction that had to earn trust, give people a clear reason to save and make every movement of money easy to understand.

WHAT WE HEARD

Trust, control and a reason to save.

“Confidence. It means that there will be a responsible party that guarantees my money.”Participant
“I like to pay my bills online because of the convenience.”Participant
“Every time I make a deposit, I get points and convert them to discount coupons.”Participant

FROM FINDING TO DESIGN

Each finding had to change a product decision.

Trust

Make a responsible, reassuring product context visible from the first touchpoint.

Purpose

Support saving goals and timely nudges so saving feels intentional, not abstract.

Control

Make transaction details, fees and history visible and easy to revisit.

Reward

Use rewards for deposits to turn regular saving into a motivating habit.

THE SOLUTION

Make saving accessible, understandable and rewarding.

No minimum balanceNo interestCash awards for regular savingCash in & out through multiple channelsDesigned for everyday convenience

MARKET RESEARCH

Meet people where their money already moves.

The research considered the payment and wallet services users already knew—Vodafone Cash, BM Wallet, QNB Wallet and MyFawry—to understand familiar behaviors around mobile transfers, deposits, withdrawals and bill payment.

USER APP

The product experience.

Key moments across saving, balance visibility and request history.

03 / ZABATHA · E‑COMMERCE

Find the right part.
Without the friction.

Research and usability testing helped simplify the path from vehicle details to a compatible spare part.

← Back to portfolio

PROJECT OVERVIEW

Make finding the right spare part feel certain.

Zabatha is a digital platform for automotive components and accessories. The redesign focused on the search-and-selection experience: helping customers locate a compatible spare part, evaluate it and add it to cart with confidence.

THE PROBLEM

Customers could not reliably get from “I need a part” to the right product.

01

Some participants left without completing the task because they did not know where to start.

02

Search results and filters produced inaccurate or irrelevant results.

03

Missing car model-year context made compatibility difficult to judge.

04

Product details did not give enough information to make a confident choice.

USABILITY STUDY

Test a real product-finding task.

The research assessed usability and information findability across Zabatha’s search and selection flow.

Scenario

Find a petrol pump for your car, browse suitable results, read product details and reviews, select the right item and add it to cart.

Easy searchingClear item detailsSelect & add to cart

KEY INSIGHTS

Search needed better structure, not more options.

Insight 01

Information hierarchy was unclear.

Labels, layout and grouping did not help people navigate to the right area.

Insight 02

Filtering had to start earlier.

People needed relevant filters from the beginning: brand, model, year, engine type and category.

Insight 03

Compatibility must be visible.

Model, year, availability and product detail should be scannable before customers commit.

DESIGN RESPONSE

A better path to the exact part.

01

Search & filters

Make search prominent and guide people through applicable vehicle and product filters.

02

Result cards

Show model and year information, item availability and a clear add-to-cart state.

03

Product details

Present technical information, reviews and key item context in a more usable hierarchy.

ORIGINAL PRODUCT UI

Browse, filter, decide.

These are original screens from the redesigned product: the home discovery experience, search results and detailed product information.

04 / MONSOOQ · GAMING

Play what fits.
Pay your way.

A gaming discovery and subscription experience shaped around how players find, evaluate and access content.

← Back to portfolio
Role
UX research, product strategy, UI
Audience
Players aged 18–35
Platform
Digital gaming service

THE OPPORTUNITY

Gaming access should feel as flexible as gaming itself.

Monsooq explored a B2C service for digital games and content. The product direction centered on easy discovery and time-based entertainment for players who do not want a long-term commitment before trying something new.

DiscoverChoose a planStart playing

RESEARCH SIGNALS

Three behaviors shaped the product direction.

The interviews, competitive review and card-sorting work focused on what makes access to games feel convenient, relevant and worth returning to.

01

Payment needs to meet local reality.

Players raised regional payment constraints and the need for options beyond a single card-based path. The experience needed to support familiar, flexible payment choices.

02

Discovery starts with what is relevant now.

Players expected trending content, offers and recommendations that reflected their interests—not an undifferentiated library.

03

A trial lowers the barrier to play.

Free games, promotions and low-commitment entry points were important reasons for people to sign up and explore a new platform.

PLAYER PERSPECTIVE

From “what should I play?” to a confident first choice.

Players need relevant discovery, flexible access and low-risk ways to try content before committing.

Research synthesis · flexible access, relevant discovery and low-risk trials

DESIGN RESPONSE

Make discovery, relevance and commitment visible.

  1. 01

    Trending first

    Bring timely and popular titles forward so the service has a clear starting point.

  2. 02

    Recommendations with a reason

    Group content into recognizable recommendations rather than leaving players to search a flat catalogue.

  3. 03

    Plans that explain the trade-off

    Use clear tiering, trial access and visible benefits to make commitment easier to evaluate.

PRODUCT EXPERIENCE

Discover. Decide.
Start playing.

Discovery, recommendations and plan selection bring the product direction into focus.

05 / GO BUS · TRAVEL EXPERIENCE

Keep every ticket
in the traveller’s control.

A mobile usability study uncovered a critical gap after booking: travellers could not clearly change or cancel a trip. The redesign brought those decisions into the ticket itself.

← Back to portfolio
Role
UX research, usability testing, product design
Method
Mobile usability testing
Participants
4 participants
Focus
Booking, trip edits & cancellation
THE DESIGN QUESTION

After buying a ticket, can a traveller confidently find the right trip and understand what can still be changed?

/ 01

THE CONTEXT

The journey did not end at checkout.

The study followed a round-trip booking on mobile, from choosing buses and seats through reservation details. The most consequential usability issues appeared after booking, when people needed to manage a ticket they already owned.

STUDY TASK

Book a round trip from Cairo to Port Said, then return later to review and manage the booking.

/ 02

USABILITY STUDY

Four sessions exposed the same control gap.

Participants were asked to complete a round-trip booking on mobile. Sessions surfaced recurring confusion around trip information, seat confirmation, account access and the ability to edit or cancel.

4 / 4

Could not find trip changes

Participants expected a way to edit or cancel a booked ticket, but the available ticket view did not make those actions discoverable.

4 / 4

Trip information felt wrong

All four sessions recorded an issue with trip details shown during booking, making it harder to trust the reservation.

3 / 4

Seat confirmation was unclear

The seat step did not clearly explain the next decision and could lead people to end the booking early.

4 / 4

Sign-in interrupted the flow

The research notes describe an error during sign-up or login that caused participants to leave the app.

Counts reflect four usability sessions; they are directional findings, not population estimates.

/ 03

THE PIVOT

Make post-booking actions part of the ticket.

The core problem was not only whether editing or cancellation was possible. Travellers could not see the available actions, understand the booking conditions, or tell what would happen next.

01

Find the right trip

Use ticket identity and trip details to help people locate the reservation they want to manage.

02

Understand the consequence

Keep timing, eligibility and refund rules visible before a traveller confirms a change.

03

Confirm the result

Show a clear completion state after changing a time, a seat or cancelling a ticket.

/ 04

DESIGN RESPONSE

Redesign the ticket around the next useful action.

01

Rework ticket hierarchy

Bring the route, date, departure details, booking reference and ticket status into a clearer structure.

02

Expose trip management

Give travellers a path to edit the trip time, change seats or cancel from the booking-management flow.

03

Explain before confirming

Present the cancellation fee and refund condition before the final confirmation, then acknowledge completion.

04

Make booking steps legible

Clarify seat availability and make trip information consistent across search, ticket details and management.

/ 05

ORIGINAL PRODUCT UI

From ticket list
to trip management.

Six mobile frames cover ticket discovery, schedule search, trip details and seat selection.
